messages.author: cf47bbe63da1f3ae
messages.subject: Model compilation error - out of memory
parts:
On Win8 64 bit Stan 2.7 binary from CRAN. The model involves latent variables and a lot of parameters, runs fine for small amounts of data, but fails during compilation as more subjects are added. Memory usage of the ccplus executable during compilation hits around 1.3gb (the system has plenty to spare) and then eventually it bugs out.
Based on http://stackoverflow.com/questions/29194247/how-to-diagnose-g-error-cc1plus-exe-out-of-memory-allocating-838860800-bytes
I believe it could be a mismatch of encoding type? Perhaps the error is related more specifically to my system, but the above link makes me think it may be something stan is doing.

Error in compileCode(f, code, language = language, verbose = verbose) : 
  Compilation ERROR, function(s)/method(s) not created! 
cc1plus.exe: out of memory allocating 1834816 bytes
make: *** [file216c36ee1b41.o] Error 1
Warning message:
running command 'make -f "C:/PROGRA~1/R/R-32~1.0/etc/x64/Makeconf" -f "C:/PROGRA~1/R/R-32~1.0/share/make/winshlib.mk" -f "C:/Users/Charlie/Documents/.R/Makevars" SHLIB_LDFLAGS='$(SHLIB_CXXLDFLAGS)' SHLIB_LD='$(SHLIB_CXXLD)' SHLIB="file216c36ee1b41.dll" WIN=64 TCLBIN=64 OBJECTS="file216c36ee1b41.o"' had status 2 
In addition: Warning message:
running command 'C:/PROGRA~1/R/R-32~1.0/bin/x64/R CMD SHLIB file216c36ee1b41.cpp 2> file216c36ee1b41.cpp.err.txt' had status 1

>

messages.author: ab7b24da45678eac
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Model compilation error - out of memory
parts:
It looks like that it takes forever to compile this C++ code this your model using Clang on Mac, so for now I can only suggest simplifying the model. 


I think it wasn’t a crash for you (I mean not crushing R).  It’s just the C++ compiler on Windows that cannot compiler the C++ and then it  stops.  The C++ compiler in Rtools on windows itself is a 32 bit program, so it can use at most 4G memory (in fact I guess it’s less than 4G) and it is easy to abort compiling.  

Jiqiang

messages.author: cf47bbe63da1f3ae
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Model compilation error - out of memory
parts:
Ok, too much abuse it seems :) I didn't seem to be reaching any 4gb limit on my attempts, it seemed to peak at most around 1.6gb. 50 minutes compiling seems impressive, given that for models I can compile (say, half the attached size) it only takes 1 or 2 mins. I will go back and have a think how I can specify it better. Any suggestions for efficient specifications of a series of matrices that have some parameters fixed to a single value across all subjects and some parameters free for each subject? Then also estimating the covariance matrix for all free parameters?  Here's some example model with just the relevant bits, in this case for only a single matrix, DRIFT, but typically I'd like 8 or so matrices per individual. Let me know if more commenting / explanation would help.

data {
  int<lower=1> nmanifest; // here 2
  int<lower=1> nlatent; // here 2
  int<lower=1> nsubjects; //here 3 subjects
  int<lower=0> nparams; // here 3 free params per subject
  matrix[nlatent,nlatent] DRIFTvalues; // here a 2*2
  matrix[nparams,nparams] IIparams; // here a 3*3 identity
}

parameters {
  cov_matrix[nparams] hypervariance; //  the hyper covariance of all subject level parameters (in this case 3 drift parameters per individual, so a 3*3)

  vector[nparams] hypermeans; // the hyper means for each drift parameter
 
  real i1_drift11; // free parameters for each individuals drift matrices
  real i2_drift11;
  real i3_drift11;
  real i1_drift21;
  real i2_drift21;
  real i3_drift21;
  real i1_drift22;
  real i2_drift22;
  real i3_drift22;
}

transformed parameters {
  matrix[nlatent,nlatent] DRIFT[nsubjects]; // the individuals drift matrices

  vector[nparams] indparams[nsubjects];  //this collects all free parameters per subject into a vector, so the covariance can be estimated

  indparams[1,1] <- i1_drift11;
  indparams[1,2] <- i1_drift21;
  indparams[1,3] <- i1_drift22;
  indparams[2,1] <- i2_drift11;
  indparams[2,2] <- i2_drift21;
  indparams[2,3] <- i2_drift22;
  indparams[3,1] <- i3_drift11;
  indparams[3,2] <- i3_drift21;
  indparams[3,3] <- i3_drift22;
 
  DRIFT[1][1,1] <- i1_drift11; //putting the free and fixed params into each subjects matrices
  DRIFT[1][1,2] <- DRIFTvalues[1,2];
  DRIFT[1][2,1] <- i1_drift21;
  DRIFT[1][2,2] <- i1_drift22;
  DRIFT[2][1,1] <- i2_drift11;
  DRIFT[2][1,2] <- DRIFTvalues[1,2];
  DRIFT[2][2,1] <- i2_drift21;
  DRIFT[2][2,2] <- i2_drift22;
  DRIFT[3][1,1] <- i3_drift11;
  DRIFT[3][1,2] <- DRIFTvalues[1,2];
  DRIFT[3][2,1] <- i3_drift21;
  DRIFT[3][2,2] <- i3_drift22; 
}

model { 
  hypervariance ~ inv_wishart(11,IIparams);

  for(hypermeani in 1:nparams){
    hypermeans[hypermeani] ~ normal(0,10);
  }
 
  indparams ~ multi_normal(hypermeans, hypervariance);
}

On Friday, July 24, 2015 at 9:05:42 PM UTC+2, Bob Carpenter wrote:
Yes, because of the general question of how to
deal with partially specified data structures.  Don't worry
about efficiency --- loops and assignment are very fast
in Stan and will be dominated by operations that require
derivatives.

- Bob

I will go back and have a think how I can specify it better. Any suggestions for efficient specifications of a series of matrices that have some parameters fixed to a single value across all subjects and some parameters free for each subject? Then also estimating the covariance matrix for all free parameters?  Here's some example model with just the relevant bits, in this case for only a single matrix, DRIFT, but typically I'd like 8 or so matrices per individual. Let me know if more commenting / explanation would help.

> >   matrix[nparams,nparams] IIparams; // here a 3*3 identity

> >   cov_matrix[nparams] hypervariance; //  the hyper covariance of all subject level parameters (in this case 3 drift parameters per individual, so a 3*3)

> >  
> >   real i1_drift11; // free parameters for each individuals drift matrices

> >   real i2_drift21;
> >   real i3_drift21;
> >   real i1_drift22;
> >   real i2_drift22;
> >   real i3_drift22;
> >  
> > }
> >
> > transformed parameters {
> >
> >   matrix[nlatent,nlatent] DRIFT[nsubjects]; // the individuals drift matrices
> >
> >   vector[nparams] indparams[nsubjects];  //this collects all free parameters per subject into a vector, so the covariance can be estimated
> >
> >   indparams[1,1] <- i1_drift11;
> >   indparams[1,2] <- i1_drift21;
> >   indparams[1,3] <- i1_drift22;
> >   indparams[2,1] <- i2_drift11;
> >   indparams[2,2] <- i2_drift21;

> >   indparams[3,2] <- i3_drift21;
> >   indparams[3,3] <- i3_drift22;
> >  
> >   DRIFT[1][1,1] <- i1_drift11; //putting the free and fixed params into each subjects matrices
> >   DRIFT[1][1,2] <- DRIFTvalues[1,2];
> >   DRIFT[1][2,1] <- i1_drift21;
> >   DRIFT[1][2,2] <- i1_drift22;
> >   DRIFT[2][1,1] <- i2_drift11;
> >   DRIFT[2][1,2] <- DRIFTvalues[1,2];
> >   DRIFT[2][2,1] <- i2_drift21;
> >   DRIFT[2][2,2] <- i2_drift22;
> >   DRIFT[3][1,1] <- i3_drift11;
> >   DRIFT[3][1,2] <- DRIFTvalues[1,2];
> >   DRIFT[3][2,1] <- i3_drift21;
> >   DRIFT[3][2,2] <- i3_drift22;
> >
> >  
> > }
> >

> > model {

> >   hypervariance ~ inv_wishart(11,IIparams);
> >   for(hypermeani in 1:nparams){
> >     hypermeans[hypermeani] ~ normal(0,10);
> >   }
> >  
> >   indparams ~ multi_normal(hypermeans, hypervariance);

messages.author: cab04b8f0759c712
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Model compilation error - out of memory
parts:
Hi Charles,

Clearly, this code has been generated. Some comments inline.
On Fri, Jul 24, 2015 at 4:33 PM, Ben Goodrich <goodri...@gmail.com> wrote:

Put the scalars into long vectors or arrays.

Ben

Yup. Listen to Ben. No reason you need to have 100 x i*_drift_eta1_eta1 parameters, followed by 100 x i*_cint_eta1 parameters, and so on. What's the significance of the number 100? It's used all over the place. Could you not generalize to a vector?

On Friday, July 24, 2015 at 4:24:19 PM UTC-4, Charles Driver wrote:
Right, but efficiency in terms of minimising  numbers of variables / transformed variables, so the compiler can handle it...

We haven't done any optimization of the generated C++ code using stanc. It translates things line for line (roughly).

I think this is a case where you just need to be more clever about what you want to do. If you haven't noticed yet, the generated Stan program isn't safe. For example, nparams is data, hypermeans is declared as a transformed parameter "vector[nparams] hypermeans", but elements 1 -- 11 are assigned directly.


My suggestion is to sit down and think about what this would look like with vectors or arrays. That'll reduce your C++ compiler burden enough, I think. Of course, you'll have difficulty at runtime, but if you can't compile, you won't get there.


Daniel
